section_summary: This section centers on the 1930 London Naval Treaty: Japanese press reactions, Diet debates over naval strength and constitutional authority, and a later report on Japan’s naval replenishment program. It also contains correspondence about an attempt to sell alleged secret plans of the battleship Mutsu to a U.S. vice consul in Seoul, followed by treaty notifications concerning the destroyer Sagiri. The final despatch begins a longer account of Diet debates and continues beyond page 75.

subfiles.title: Index note on Japanese purchase of ammonia hydrate
subfiles.about: Points to Melbourne reports on ammonia hydrate purchased for the Japanese Navy.
subfiles.summary: Refers readers to three confidential Melbourne reports about the Japanese Navy’s purchase.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on constitutional authority over the navy
subfiles.about: Points to a report on claims that the London Naval Treaty infringed naval command powers.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references a report on the government’s constitutional right to limit naval strength by treaty.

subfiles.title: Japanese reaction and constitutional dispute over the London Naval Treaty
subfiles.about: Reports changing Japanese opinion and a dispute over the government’s authority to sign the London Naval Treaty.
subfiles.summary: The embassy observes growing press support for the treaty even as opposition politicians challenge the government’s authority to accept naval limits without Naval Staff approval. It reviews Diet exchanges, constitutional arguments concerning the emperor’s powers and military command, and prospects for Privy Council ratification. It also discusses possible restraint in replacement construction and encloses editorials, Shidehara’s address, and a Diet debate account.

subfiles.title: The Success of the London Conference: Example of Political Solution
subfiles.about: Praises political compromise among Britain, the United States, and Japan at the naval conference.
subfiles.summary: The editorial calls the impending agreement a major success despite limits on disarmament. It presents British and American cruiser concessions, and U.S. flexibility toward Japan, as evidence that negotiation can replace naval competition.

subfiles.title: Signature of the Five-Power Naval Treaty
subfiles.about: Assesses shortcomings of the newly signed naval treaty.
subfiles.summary: The editorial faults the limited reduction of auxiliary ships, the absence of French and Italian tonnage agreements, and Japan’s cruiser and submarine allotments.

subfiles.title: The Conclusion of the Naval Treaty
subfiles.about: Welcomes the treaty as progress toward limits on auxiliary warships.
subfiles.summary: The editorial celebrates the agreement despite its imperfect ratios and incomplete French and Italian participation. It stresses the value of restraining competition and expects future conferences to settle outstanding questions.

subfiles.title: The Signing of the London Treaty
subfiles.about: Supports the treaty while urging restraint in optional cruiser and replacement construction.
subfiles.summary: The editorial welcomes limits on competition and savings from delaying capital-ship replacement. It warns that American construction of three additional heavy cruisers or extensive Japanese replacement building could weaken the treaty’s disarmament purpose and burden taxpayers.

subfiles.title: Naval Limitation Treaty Signed
subfiles.about: Reviews the negotiations and Japan’s concessions in securing the treaty.
subfiles.summary: The editorial traces Anglo-American preparations and Japan’s cooperation at London, including concessions on heavy cruisers and submarines. It acknowledges modest savings and incomplete auxiliary-ship reductions but urges public support for peace and further disarmament.

subfiles.title: Five-Power Treaty Signed
subfiles.about: Welcomes naval reductions while identifying risks to the treaty.
subfiles.summary: The editorial praises reduced tonnage and deferred capital-ship replacement, but questions Japan’s future freedom of action and the lack of binding French and Italian limits.

subfiles.title: Baron Shidehara’s address on foreign policy and the naval treaty
subfiles.about: Prints Shidehara’s Diet address on trade negotiations and the London Naval Treaty.
subfiles.summary: Shidehara discusses China’s tariff autonomy, commercial agreements, and the naval treaty. He defends Japan’s decision to accept the treaty and its provision for limited early ship replacement.

subfiles.title: The Naval Treaty: Budget Committee debate
subfiles.about: Reports Diet questions on cruiser ratios, national security, and consultation with military authorities.
subfiles.summary: Uehara and Uchida challenge government assurances; Hamaguchi and Shidehara defend the treaty.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Japanese eight-inch-gun cruisers
subfiles.about: Points to comments on Japanese heavy cruisers under construction.
subfiles.summary: References cruiser construction and Japanese allotments under Hughes’s proposal.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Japan’s naval replenishment appropriation
subfiles.about: Points to a despatch on funds allocated for Japanese naval construction.
subfiles.summary: Notes that calling the 1931–36 naval construction allocation a treaty saving is misleading.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Japan’s naval replenishment program
subfiles.about: Points to another report on the Japanese naval replenishment program.
subfiles.summary: Identifies a related report and notes that a copy is attached.

subfiles.title: Agreement on Japan’s naval replenishment program
subfiles.about: Reports a government–navy agreement on spending and ship construction after the London Treaty.
subfiles.summary: The despatch outlines planned warships, naval aviation, and modernization expenditure. It judges the settlement a political success for Hamaguchi and Inoue in their dispute with naval authorities.

subfiles.title: Attempted sale of alleged Mutsu plans
subfiles.from: W. Cameron Forbes, U.S. Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports arrests following an offer to sell alleged secret battleship plans to Vice Consul Stephan.
subfiles.summary: Forbes praises Stephan for declining the offer and informing Japanese authorities. He notes concern that press accounts could falsely suggest U.S. interest in the plans.

subfiles.title: Consul General Davis’s report on the alleged Mutsu plans
subfiles.from: John K. Davis, U.S. Consulate General, Seoul
subfiles.about: Transmits Stephan’s memoranda, correspondence, and press clippings about the attempted sale.
subfiles.summary: Davis recounts the confidential referral to Government-General officials and later press reports, promising to report further coverage.

subfiles.title: Stephan’s confidential letter to Oda
subfiles.about: Forwards information about Kiyoshi Hasegawa and requests discretion.
subfiles.summary: Stephan asks that neither he nor the consulate be identified in any action.

subfiles.title: Stephan’s memorandum on Hasegawa’s offer
subfiles.about: Records Hasegawa’s offer to sell alleged plans of the battleship Mutsu.
subfiles.summary: Stephan describes Hasegawa’s visit, rejects the proposed sale, and records his account of how an acquaintance in Tokyo obtained the alleged plans.

subfiles.title: Oda’s acknowledgment of Stephan’s report
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the confidential report about Hasegawa.
subfiles.summary: Oda says he referred the matter to the responsible department and promises discretion.

subfiles.title: Stephan’s memorandum on press disclosure
subfiles.about: Records Oda’s visit and press inquiries concerning the Hasegawa case.
subfiles.summary: Stephan notes Oda’s surprise at publication and a reporter’s questions to consulate staff.

subfiles.title: Possible testimony by Vice Consul Stephan
subfiles.from: W. Cameron Forbes, U.S. Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Seeks the Department’s view on Stephan’s possible appearance at a public trial.
subfiles.summary: Forbes forwards Davis’s request and the embassy’s advice, asking for telegraphic instructions if Stephan should avoid appearing.

subfiles.title: Davis requests instructions on Stephan’s testimony
subfiles.about: Requests instructions should Japanese authorities call Stephan as a witness.
subfiles.summary: Davis seeks guidance after a newspaper reports that the case will proceed to public trial.

subfiles.title: Embassy guidance on consular testimony
subfiles.from: Eugene H. Dooman, for the ambassador
subfiles.about: Advises how Stephan should respond if asked to testify.
subfiles.summary: Dooman favors cooperation where Stephan’s appearance is needed for justice, while suggesting testimony at the consulate if acceptable. He advises avoiding coercive summons language.

subfiles.title: Department telegram on Stephan’s testimony and publicity
subfiles.about: Gives instructions on testimony and adverse publicity in the Hasegawa case.
subfiles.summary: The Department discourages publicity but says Stephan must testify if required; it permits informal representations to correct false reports.

subfiles.title: Assurance that Stephan will not testify
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, U.S. Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports an assurance that Stephan will not be called as a trial witness.
subfiles.summary: Neville forwards Davis’s despatch and Stephan’s account of further discussions with Government-General officials.

subfiles.title: Davis forwards Stephan’s account of official assurances
subfiles.about: Transmits a memorandum on Government-General officials’ response to the case.
subfiles.summary: Davis expects no further developments affecting the consulate.

subfiles.title: Stephan’s memorandum on Hozumi’s visit
subfiles.about: Records an apology for press disclosure and assurances about the trial.
subfiles.summary: Hozumi apologizes for the publicity, says Stephan will not be called as a witness, and promises closed proceedings. Stephan also raises concern about possible retaliation.

subfiles.title: Japanese notification of destroyer Sagiri’s completion
subfiles.about: Supplies particulars of the completed destroyer Sagiri under the London Naval Treaty.
subfiles.summary: Reports Sagiri’s completion date, classification, displacement, and dimensions.

subfiles.title: State Department forwards Sagiri particulars
subfiles.about: Forwards the Japanese notification about the destroyer Sagiri.
subfiles.summary: Encloses the ambassador’s note for the Navy’s information.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Japanese Sagiri notification
subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of Sagiri’s treaty particulars.
subfiles.summary: Stimson thanks Debuchi for the March 18 notification.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Diet debates over the London Naval Treaty
subfiles.about: Points to a report on Diet debates and related treaty issues.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references a despatch on discussion of the treaty in the Diet.

subfiles.title: Diet debates on the London Naval Treaty
subfiles.about: Reviews Diet debate on the treaty, naval estimates, and the government’s authority over military strength.
subfiles.summary: The despatch explains how treaty questions were raised in both houses and their budget committees, distinguishing opposition tactics in the lower house from concern expressed by peers. It recounts Shidehara’s defense of the treaty as a way to prevent escalating cruiser construction and notes his rejection of claims that Japan had been pressured into unacceptable terms. The document continues after page 75.
